To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the optimal actuator-sensors placement problem for linear time-invariant (LTI) dynamical systems may be solved by a polynomial time algorithm.

(i) we provide an algorithm to determine the minimal number of inputs required to achieve structural controllability of an LTI system; (ii) we characterize all possible configurations of the input matrix that achieve structural controllabilty; and (iii) the proposed solution is polynomial in the number of states of the system.
we have developed an algorithm that finds the minimum number of actuators and sensors that are required to control and observe a given system.
In summary, our research is concerned with

determining the minimum number of inputs (outputs) required to ensure structural stability, controllability, or observability of a system, while guaranteeing that each input (output) can only affect directly a single state (output) variable.

the methodology presented in this paper is a structured systems approach for solving the actuator-sensor allocation problem in LTI systems.
the proposed solution methodology is a general and efficient tool for the optimal design of dedicated actuator and sensor structures in LTI systems.
the problem of determining the minimal number of dedicated inputs (or outputs) required to ensure structural (in)controllability (or (in)observability) is solved in this work.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a structured systems approach for the optimal actuator/sensor placement problem in linear time invariant systems.
we provide a methodology to optimally design the structure of an input matrix (and its dual, the output matrix) for a given autonomous linear dynamical structure.
we present a methodology to determine a minimum structure of the input/output matrix for LTI systems such that the system becomes structurally controllable/observably.
The main takeaway from our work is that

by judiciously selecting the structure of the minimal B and C matrices, we can significantly reduce the number of actuators and sensors, respectively, while preserving the desired structural properties.
the proposed methodology is applicable for the design of the minimal input and output matrices in a wide range of systems, including, for example, the design of a networked control system (NCS).

the proposed approach provides a structured framework to solve the actuator/sensors allocation problem for LTI systems, and that this approach may be readily extended for the solution of other problems of similar nature.
